traveler: Empress Theodora (Theodora Augusta, consort of Justinian I)
title: The Stool and the Purple: from the Sand of the Hippodrome to the Mausoleum of the Emperors
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Constantinople, the death of the Master of the Bears
stops.date_confidence: inferred. Procopius gives no year: Acacius dies somewhere in the reign of Anastasius, 491 to 518, and 0500 is set only to order the segment. Theodora's own birth is unrecorded, with modern estimates clustering c. 495-500 and Constantinople the strongest inference rather than an attested place.
stops.campa: Acacius keeps the bears for the Green faction of the Hippodrome, and when he dies under Anastasius he leaves a widow and three small daughters: Comito, Theodora, Anastasia. The office is a livelihood, not an honour, and it does not pass to girls. The dancing master of the Greens, Asterius, takes a bribe and gives the bear-keeping to another man. The pay stops that month. In the house there are three girls, none of them ten years old, and a widow with no trade the city will pay her for.
stops.quote: There was in Byzantium a certain Acacius, keeper of the animals used in the circus, an adherent of the Green Faction.
suggested_refs: The kathisma and the beast-pens of the Hippodrome of Constantinople, under the modern Sultanahmet square
sources: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 9, Dewing text at penelope.uchicago.edu
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora' (roman-emperors.sites.luc.edu/dora.htm)

stops.name: The Hippodrome, the three garlanded children
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the scene is attested but undated, and 0505 orders the segment. Procopius's reading of this afternoon as the origin of Theodora's lifelong Blue partisanship and hatred of the Greens is his own retrospective psychology.
stops.campa: The mother crowns the three girls with garlands and sends them out onto the sand as suppliants, into the middle of the circus, before the assembled Greens. The Greens look at them and refuse. The refusal is public and is meant to be. The Blues, whose own Master of the Bears has lately died, take the office and the family with it. Theodora is perhaps eight years old, standing on the racing sand in a garland while one half of the arena looks past her and the other half calls her family over.
suggested_refs: The spina and racing floor of the Hippodrome, where suppliants were shown to the assembled factions
sources: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 9, Dewing text at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: The Hippodrome, the stool on her shoulders
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the detail is attested verbatim in Procopius but carries no date.
stops.campa: Comito is the first to go on the stage and the first to succeed at it. Theodora, still too young for a part of her own, walks behind her sister in a little sleeved tunic, carrying on her shoulders the stool her sister is accustomed to sit on. She is a servant to a servant of the crowd, and it is the only picture of her childhood that anyone has: a small girl walking behind her sister, carrying the furniture. The detail comes from Procopius, who sets it down decades later in order to shame her.
suggested_refs: The theatrical quarters attached to the Blue faction at the Hippodrome
sources: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 9, Dewing text at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: The theatres of Constantinople, the girl on the stage
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to particulars. No venue is named in any source and the coordinate is an approximate placement in the theatre district beside the Hippodrome. Procopius's account of her act, including the routine with geese and scattered grain, is singularly attested in a hostile posthumous invective and is not corroborated anywhere.
stops.campa: She grows into the mime theatre, the low comic stage whose actresses are infames in law and are received in no respectable house. Procopius says she sold her youthful beauty to whoever came along, plying her trade with practically her whole body, and sets down an obscene routine with geese and scattered grain in full detail. He is the only witness and he is writing to destroy her. What is not in doubt is the legal class she belonged to: an actress, and therefore a woman forbidden to marry a senator.
stops.quote: For the girl had not a particle of modesty, nor did any man ever see her embarrassed.
suggested_refs: The Roman theatre district of Constantinople, north-east of the Hippodrome
sources: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 9, Dewing text at penelope.uchicago.edu
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

segments.name: The Road East and the Return

stops.name: The Pentapolis, in the household of Hecebolus
stops.date_confidence: inferred. Procopius gives no date. The seat is uncertain: the coordinate is Ptolemais, but by the sixth century Ptolemais had decayed and had been replaced as capital of the province, so Apollonia may well have been the governor's residence. The place is therefore approximate at province level, not at city level.
stops.campa: Hecebolus of Tyre takes the governorship of Libya Pentapolis and takes Theodora with him across the sea, the first time she leaves the city she was born in. Procopius says she followed in his train and served him in the most shameful capacity. Whatever the arrangement was, it ends: she gives him offence, and the governor puts her out of his house in a province where she knows nobody and has no claim on anyone. She is somewhere on the African shore, months of sailing from the Hippodrome.
stops.quote: Later she was following in the train of Hecebolus, a Tyrian, who had taken over the administration of Pentapolis.
suggested_refs: The ruined provincial cities of the Cyrenaican Pentapolis: Ptolemais, Apollonia, Cyrene
sources: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 9, Dewing text at penelope.uchicago.edu
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'
Wikipedia, 'Ptolemais, Cyrenaica' (for the coordinate and the decay of the seat)

stops.name: Alexandria, the whole East before her
stops.date_confidence: the Alexandria leg is attested verbatim in Procopius; the year is inference only.
stops.campa: Cast off in Africa, she goes to Alexandria. The text is bare. She first went to Alexandria, it says, and later, after making the round of the whole East, she made her way back to Byzantium. Between those two clauses lie perhaps three years and several thousand miles, travelled by a discarded actress with no money and no protector. How she paid for any of it, and who she went with, is recorded nowhere. The middle of the sentence is the middle of her life.
suggested_refs: The harbour and Christian quarters of sixth-century Alexandria
sources: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 9, Dewing text at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Alexandria, the patriarch and the other creed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A meeting with the Miaphysite patriarch Timothy III/IV is a modern inference read backward from her later church politics; no contemporary text documents it, and neither the date nor the depth of any relationship is recorded.
stops.campa: Alexandria in these years is the capital of the anti-Chalcedonian world, crowded with monks and with bishops driven out of Syria, and its patriarch Timothy holds the see against the emperor's creed. Tradition puts Theodora in front of him. Nothing contemporary records the meeting. The whole of it is reconstructed backward from what she does afterward, which is to shelter exactly these men, and their successors, for the rest of her life. She arrives in the city a ruined provincial mistress and there is no account of what she is when she leaves it.
suggested_refs: The patriarchal see of Alexandria under Timothy III/IV, centre of the anti-Chalcedonian communion
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: Antioch, the dancer Macedonia
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Antioch is not in Anecdota 9, which names only Alexandria and 'the whole East'; the Antioch leg and the dancer Macedonia enter through Secret History 12 as relayed by the DIR biography. The claim that Macedonia was an informant for Justinian is uncorroborated hostile anecdote.
stops.campa: At Antioch a dancer named Macedonia helps her, or so Procopius says, and he adds that Macedonia was already sending news of the East to Justinian in the capital. On this one line a whole literature has been built in which Theodora is a spy, and the line will not carry it. Two women of the stage sit in a room in Antioch, one of them settled there, one just off the road from Alexandria, and a letter goes from that room to a man in the capital. Whether Theodora knew what was in it, the text does not say.
suggested_refs: The theatre and hippodrome quarter of Antioch on the Orontes, before the earthquakes of 526 and 528
sources: Procopius, Secret History 12, as summarized in Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: Constantinople, the small house and the wool
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The wool-spinning is carried by the DIR biography as later tradition and is not in Procopius, Anecdota 9, where the researcher searched for it twice and did not find it. The research pool attributed it to Procopius in error; the attribution is corrected here to tradition.
stops.campa: She comes back to the city that threw her out, and takes a small house near the palace. The story that she lived quietly there and kept herself by spinning wool is the one detail of her early life that flatters her, and it is the one detail no hostile source supplies. Somebody wanted the empress to have had a virtuous interval before the crown, and somebody supplied her with one. Wool or no wool, she is back in the city, in a rented house a few streets below the palace, and the man who governs the empire in his uncle's name lives inside it.
suggested_refs: The lodging-quarters below the Great Palace, between the Hippodrome and the sea walls
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora' (carrying the tradition)

segments.name: The Law of the Repentant Actress

stops.name: The Great Palace, raised to patrician rank
stops.date_confidence: attested that Justinian raised her to patrician rank; the date is inference and orders the segment.
stops.campa: Justinian is the emperor's nephew and his heir in all but name, a Latin-speaking peasant's son out of Illyricum who has made himself the most powerful man in the East without wearing the crown. He sees her, and Procopius writes that he conceived for her an overpowering love and at first knew her as a mistress. That much is the ordinary arrangement between a great man and an actress, and it goes no further than a household. Then he has her made patricia, a rank of the high aristocracy, held in her own name and not in his.
stops.quote: Justinian conceived for her an overpowering love; and at first he knew her as a mistress.
suggested_refs: The Great Palace of Constantinople, seat of the heir's household under Justin I
sources: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 9, Dewing text at penelope.uchicago.edu
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Great Palace, the law rewritten for one woman
stops.date_confidence: attested as a text, undated in itself. The constitution is Codex Justinianus V.4.23, dated by the DIR biography to between 520 and 523 and said to follow the death of the empress Euphemia; the research pool's date of 524 is wrong and is corrected here. Note the unresolved tension: the same source elsewhere places Euphemia's death about 523, which would leave the constitution almost no room before it.
stops.campa: Roman law forbids a man of senatorial rank to marry a woman who has been on the stage. A constitution goes out under Justin's name permitting a repentant actress raised to high dignity by imperial grant to marry whom she pleases, the former life cancelled by the grant. It is drafted as general legislation for all such women. It fits exactly one couple. A general law is the politest available way to make a private exception. The bar Theodora was born under is not argued around. It is repealed.
suggested_refs: Codex Justinianus V.4.23, the constitution on the marriage of women raised from the stage
sources: David Daube, 'The Marriage of Justinian and Theodora,' Catholic University Law Review 16 (1967)
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Great Palace, the objection of the empress Euphemia
stops.date_confidence: reported, not independently documented. Euphemia's opposition and the marriage's delay until after her death come through the DIR biography summarizing Procopius; the year of her death is not firmly fixed.
stops.campa: Euphemia, wife of Justin, was bought as a slave and freed, and was his concubine before she was his empress. She is the one person at court with the standing to object, and she objects. The sources record no argument of hers, only the refusal. She is fond of her nephew, they say, and she will not have this woman in the family, and no other objection from that court is reported at all. Justinian does not force the marriage past his aunt and does not give up the woman either. He waits.
suggested_refs: The women's apartments of the Great Palace under Justin I
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora', summarizing Procopius

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the marriage in the older church
stops.date_confidence: attested as 524 or 525; the day is unrecorded and 1 January is a placeholder. The venue is inferred: the cathedral of that moment is the Theodosian Hagia Sophia, which burns in 532, and not the building standing on the site today.
stops.campa: The patriarch Epiphanius joins them in the cathedral, a colonnaded basilica of Theodosius, the third church on the ground, that will burn to its foundations within eight years. The bear-keeper's daughter marries the heir of the Roman empire. Nothing about the ceremony is irregular, because the law was altered first, which is the entire point of the altering. The patriarch is the patriarch of the capital and the rite is the ordinary rite. The year is 524 or 525; the day of it nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The Theodosian Hagia Sophia, whose carved entrance lintels survive in the excavation beside the present church
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Great Palace, proclaimed Augusta
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 April 527.
stops.campa: On the first of April the old emperor, sick and failing, crowns his nephew co-emperor beside him, and Theodora is proclaimed Augusta in the same hour. She is not a consort admitted to the ceremonial by courtesy: she is crowned, and she holds the title in her own name, and the acclamations name her. Within eight years her husband will write into the preamble of a law that he consulted her before making it. The old emperor, who has reigned nine years and is being carried through the ceremony, has four months to live.
suggested_refs: The Augustaion and the ceremonial approaches of the Great Palace, where the acclamations were made
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'
Justinian, Novel 8, preface (droitromain.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr)

stops.name: The Great Palace, the death of Justin I
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 August 527.
stops.campa: Justin I dies on the first of August, four months after the coronation. Justinian means to take the West back from the Goths and the Vandals, to rewrite the whole of Roman law, and to force one creed on a church that has been split for two generations. He gets the first two. He does not get the third, and for the twenty-one years his wife is alive she shelters the losing party in her own quarter of the palace, without ever contradicting him in public.
suggested_refs: The imperial mausoleum of Justin I at the Church of the Holy Apostles
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Great Palace, Comito married to the general Sittas
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the weakest item in this file. The marriage is followed from Procopius, the date of about 528 is not firmly attested in the sources reached, and the research pool sited the event at the Palace of Hormisdas on no authority whatever. It is placed at the imperial palace here and flagged rather than dropped.
stops.campa: Comito, who went on the stage first and whom Theodora once followed carrying her stool, is married to Sittas, general of the armies of Armenia and one of the two best soldiers Justinian has. Of the three girls sent out garlanded onto the circus sand, one is now empress and one is wife to a magister militum, and both of them got there inside twenty years of the refusal. The third, Anastasia, drops out of the record after that afternoon and is not heard of again.
suggested_refs: The command of the magister militum per Armeniam, held by Sittas in the 520s and 530s
sources: Procopius, Secret History and Wars, as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Saints Sergius and Bacchus, the inscription in the stone
stops.date_confidence: the church is dated 527-536; 0530 orders the segment. Coordinates corrected to the church itself, now Kucuk Ayasofya: the research pool carried the Hormisdas and Boukoleon point about three hundred metres east.
stops.campa: Beside the palace of Hormisdas, where the two of them lived before the crown came to them and where she will later hide bishops, they raise a church to the soldier-martyrs Sergius and Bacchus: an octagon forced into an irregular plot, carrying a ribbed dome on eight piers. Around the inside of it, cut into the marble entablature and running the whole circuit of the room, is a Greek dedication in twelve hexameters. It names the founders. Where it comes to her it reads theostephes Theodora, God-crowned.
suggested_refs: The twelve-hexameter Greek dedicatory inscription running the entablature of Kucuk Ayasofya, Istanbul
sources: The surviving Greek dedicatory inscription of the church
Wikipedia, 'Little Hagia Sophia' (dating and siting)

stops.name: The Hippodrome, the day the factions agree
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 January 532. The research pool carried 1 January, twelve days early at the chronological anchor of the whole revolt; corrected here.
stops.campa: Two condemned men, one Blue and one Green, fall from the gallows alive and take sanctuary in a church, and the city prefect will not pardon them. On the thirteenth of January the two factions come to the Hippodrome for the races and for once do not shout at each other. They shout the same word at the emperor's box. Nika, conquer, the cry with which the crowd drives on a chariot team, becomes the password of a rising that will burn the middle of Constantinople for five days.
suggested_refs: The burnt zone of central Constantinople, January 532: the senate house, the Baths of Zeuxippus, the Theodosian cathedral
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.24, Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook
Wikipedia, 'Nika riots' (for the 13 January date)

stops.name: The Great Palace, the ships at the harbour steps
stops.date_confidence: attested as an episode of the fifth day of the revolt. The speech as it stands is Procopius's own composition in classical register, not a transcript, and the closing maxim is traced to Dionysius of Syracuse; the historical nucleus, that Theodora argued against flight and prevailed, is credited.
stops.campa: The senate house is ash, the cathedral is ash, the crowd has proclaimed Hypatius emperor at the Forum of Constantine, and inside the palace the council resolves on flight. Ships are ready at the private harbour steps. Theodora speaks last, against every man in the room. It is unendurable, she says, for one who has been an emperor to become a fugitive; she cannot live a day in which she is not addressed as mistress. As for herself, she approves the old saying. Nobody boards the ships.
stops.quote: For as for myself, I approve a certain ancient saying that royalty is a good burial-shroud.
stops.quote_source: Procopius, Wars 1.24, Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook translation
suggested_refs: The Boukoleon harbour and its private imperial steps, below the Great Palace
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.24, Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: The Hippodrome, Belisarius and Mundus come in
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 January 532, the same day as Hypatius's proclamation; the research pool carried 19 January, corrected here. Procopius's figure of more than thirty thousand dead is his own. A much higher figure of eighty thousand is attributed to Pseudo-Zachariah Rhetor and could not be checked against a primary text.
stops.campa: Belisarius comes into the Hippodrome from one side with his Gothic and Herul troops. Mundus comes in through the passage the Byzantines call the Gate of Death. The crowd is packed on the tiers, unarmed, celebrating a new emperor and waiting for the games that will confirm him. The soldiers work until they are tired. Procopius counts more than thirty thousand dead in the Hippodrome on that day. A Syriac chronicle attributed to Zachariah Rhetor puts the figure at eighty thousand.
suggested_refs: The Gate of Death of the Hippodrome, through which Mundus's troops entered on 18 January 532
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.24, Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: The Great Palace, the nephews of Anastasius
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day after the massacre, which is 19 January 532; the research pool carried 20 January, corrected as a consequence of the massacre date. Whether Theodora personally insisted on the executions is later inference and is not documented.
stops.campa: Hypatius and Pompeius, nephews of the emperor Anastasius, are taken alive out of the wreck. Hypatius pleads that the crowd dragged him to the throne against his will, which happens to be true. The next day soldiers kill both men, throw the bodies into the sea, and confiscate their property to the treasury. Later writers say the empress insisted on the killings. No document says so. Some years afterward Justinian gives the confiscated estates back to the heirs of the two men, which is the last the record has to say about it.
suggested_refs: The confiscated estates of Hypatius and Pompeius, restored to their heirs by Justinian some years later
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.24, Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: Hagia Sophia, the great church out of the burnt ground
stops.date_confidence: the rebuilding runs 532 to 537; 0533 orders the segment and is not a documented date. The source crediting the imperial pair jointly is Procopius's Buildings, panegyric composed after Theodora's death, and her personal share cannot be separated from the imperial treasury.
stops.campa: Out of the burnt quarter rises the building that will stand fourteen centuries. Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus are given an open treasury and told to roof a rectangle. The riot paid for it in the sense that the riot cleared the ground, which had already carried two churches and burned twice. Procopius, who will privately call this woman a demon in human form, credits the church in public to the piety of the two of them, and writes that the dome seems to hang from heaven on a chain.
suggested_refs: The Justinianic Hagia Sophia, begun 532 and dedicated 537
sources: Procopius, Buildings, as characterized in the DIR biography (the text of Buildings was not independently fetched)
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Great Palace, Novel 8 and the consort in the preamble
stops.date_confidence: attested: the text is dated 535. The quoted phrase is from the S. P. Scott English translation, which was fetched directly.
stops.campa: Novel 8 abolishes the suffragia, the customary payments by which a man bought his provincial governorship and then squeezed the province to get the price back. In the preamble, setting out how the reform was reached, Justinian records that he discussed the matter with his most august consort whom God has given him. No other contemporary document of state names her party to a decision. The clause is one line of chancery Latin in the middle of an administrative reform, and it survives because the reform did.
stops.quote: discussed them with Our Most August Consort whom God has given Us
stops.quote_source: Justinian, Novellae Constitutiones, Novel 8, preface (535), S. P. Scott translation
suggested_refs: Justinian's Novellae Constitutiones, the legislation issued after the second edition of the Code
sources: Justinian, Novel 8, English translation at droitromain.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/Anglica/N8_Scott.htm

stops.name: The Great Palace, Novel 14 against the traffickers
stops.date_confidence: attested as legislation of 535; the month is a placeholder. The pool's supporting claim that John Malalas records enforcement against brothel-keepers in Book 18 could not be confirmed, the fetched text of Malalas reaching only Book 4. Attributing the law to Theodora is anachronistic: it is issued in Justinian's name alone.
stops.campa: Novel 14 goes after the brothel trade at its supply end: the men who ride the provinces buying poor men's daughters, binding them with contracts and with oaths they cannot read, and setting them to work in the capital. The law voids the oaths, voids the contracts, punishes the buyers, and frames the whole business as a filth to be cleaned out of the capital. Nothing in it names Theodora, and it is issued in the emperor's name, as every law is. The woman crowned beside him came off the mime stage, out of the same trade the law is written about.
suggested_refs: Novel 14 of Justinian, on procurers and the contracts by which girls were bound
sources: Justinian, Novel 14, as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Metanoia, the house across the water
stops.date_confidence: the foundation is dated only to the 530s and the month is a placeholder. The site has not been archaeologically identified: the coordinate is an approximate placement on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus and must not be read as a located ruin. The two ancient accounts of the institution, Procopius's public Buildings and his private Secret History, flatly contradict each other on whether the women were rescued or confined; the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: Across the water the imperial pair turn a palace into a house they call Metanoia, Repentance, and put into it five hundred women taken off the market-place, where they had been working at three obols, just enough to live on. In the book Procopius publishes he calls the place a rescue out of a slavery of the body. In the book he hides he calls it a prison, and says some of the women went over the height at night rather than be transformed. Both books are his.
stops.quote: she gathered together, and sending them over to the opposite mainland she confined them in the Convent of Repentance, as it is called, trying there to compel them to adopt a new manner of life.
suggested_refs: The Convent of Metanoia on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, unlocated
sources: Procopius, Secret History 17, penelope.uchicago.edu
Procopius, Buildings I.9, as contrasted in the research dossier

stops.name: The Great Palace, Anthimus made patriarch
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is dated 535 in the DIR biography; the month is a placeholder and no primary text confirming the exact date was fetched.
stops.campa: Anthimus of Trebizond is made patriarch of Constantinople, translated from another see against the canons, and nobody at that court is in any doubt whose man he is. Theodora has put on the throne of the capital a bishop who does not believe what her husband legislates. Within months he is accused of holding privately the anti-Chalcedonian Christology that the emperor's own laws condemn. The accusation is never disproved, and the appointment is of 535.
suggested_refs: The patriarchal throne of Constantinople and the canons against translation between sees
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'
Evagrius Scholasticus, as summarized in the research dossier

stops.name: Constantinople, the pope from Rome
stops.date_confidence: the deposition of Anthimus and the synod condemning him with Severus of Antioch are dated 536; the account comes through the DIR biography summarizing the conciliar record and the Liber Pontificalis, neither fetched directly.
stops.campa: Pope Agapetus arrives on an embassy for the Gothic king Theodahad and refuses communion with the patriarch of the city. Justinian threatens him with exile, and the emperor is the one who gives way. Anthimus is deposed, and a synod condemns him together with Severus of Antioch and their allies. Agapetus dies in Constantinople a few weeks later, having got everything he came for. What the city remembers is his answer to the threat: he came expecting a Christian emperor, and he has found a Diocletian.
suggested_refs: The synod of Constantinople of 536, condemning Anthimus, Severus of Antioch, and their party
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Palace of Hormisdas, the house of the exiles
stops.date_confidence: the refuge is documented for 536 and 537 onward, after the deposition of Anthimus and the arrival in exile of Theodosius of Alexandria. The research pool's date of 530 is roughly six years early and is corrected here. John of Ephesus, the source for the visits, is a confessionally invested near-contemporary writing about his own protectress.
stops.campa: Anthimus does not go into exile. He goes into the women's quarters of the palace of Hormisdas and stays there, and he is not alone in it. Theodosius, driven out of the see of Alexandria, is lodged there too, and around the pair collects a community of Syrian and Egyptian monks running from the emperor's police. Upstairs her husband legislates against these men. John of Ephesus, who was one of them, describes the empress coming down into the quarters every few days, among the unwashed ascetics and the mats on the floor, to ask their blessing.
stops.quote: the empress Theodora, a devoted member of the Monophysite party, had built and endowed at Constantinople numerous monasteries
stops.quote_source: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History, Third Part, Book 1, trans. R. Payne Smith
suggested_refs: The Palace of Hormisdas beside the Boukoleon, converted into a Miaphysite monastery in 536-537
sources: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History, Third Part, Book 1, at tertullian.org
Wikipedia, 'Little Hagia Sophia' (for the 536-537 dating of the refuge)

stops.name: The Great Palace, the deacon who would be pope
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Liber Pontificalis and Procopius connect imperial pressure, Antonina, and Belisarius to Silverius's fall, and Silverius's death on Palmaria is attested; no surviving order shows Theodora directing the case, and the alleged bargain with Vigilius is reported rather than documented. The Liber Pontificalis was not fetched directly.
stops.campa: Belisarius holds Rome against the Goths, and in Rome Pope Silverius is stripped of the pallium, put into a monk's habit, and shipped to the island of Palmaria, a rock off the Italian coast, where he dies. The deacon Vigilius, who was in Constantinople when it began, becomes pope. The story told afterward is that Theodora bought him the chair against a promise to restore Anthimus, and that once seated he did nothing of the kind. The outcome survives. The instruction does not.
suggested_refs: The island of Palmaria in the Pontine group, where Silverius died in exile
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora', summarizing the Liber Pontificalis and Procopius

segments.name: The Prefect, the Plague, the Lightless Room

stops.name: The Great Palace, the fall of John the Cappadocian
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 541. The entrapment at the estate of Rufinianae, on the Bithynian shore near Chalcedon, is described even in the comparatively sober Wars, so the outline is strongly attested; the moral colouring and Theodora's exact instructions are Procopian. This stop is sited at the palace because Theodora was not herself at Rufinianae: Antonina was.
stops.campa: The praetorian prefect has run the empire's money for a decade, hated in the provinces and protected by his usefulness, and he is Theodora's enemy. Antonina, wife of Belisarius, takes his daughter into her confidence, draws him out to the estate at Rufinianae, and leads him into saying aloud what treason would sound like, with witnesses hidden within earshot. He is stripped of office, forced into holy orders under the name Peter, and afterward exiled. Even in the Wars, Procopius tells it as a trap set by women.
suggested_refs: The suburban estate of Rufinianae on the Bithynian shore near Chalcedon
sources: Procopius, Wars and Secret History, as summarized in the DIR biography
Wikipedia, 'John the Cappadocian' (for the 541 date)

stops.name: Constantinople, the plague comes up from Egypt
stops.date_confidence: attested to 542; the month is a placeholder. No primary chronicle entry for the outbreak was independently fetched for this file.
stops.campa: The pestilence comes up through Egypt and Syria and reaches the capital in the spring. For months the city buries what it can. When the ground is used up the roofs are taken off the towers of the wall at Sycae, across the water, and the dead are put into the towers and the roofs are put back. The emperor of the reconquered world takes it in his own palace, swells with the buboes, and recovers. For some weeks in 542 the empire has no functioning head, and outside the palace the towers go on filling.
suggested_refs: The mass burials of 542 in the towers of the Galata wall at Sycae
sources: Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'
Wikipedia, 'Theodora (6th century)'

stops.name: The Great Palace, what the generals said
stops.date_confidence: the episode is dated 542; the month is a placeholder. Procopius's Secret History 4 is the source and was not independently fetched; the punitive consequences are hostile single-source allegation.
stops.campa: While Justinian lies senseless, Belisarius and Bouzes are overheard working out what the army will do if he dies, and in particular that they will not take an emperor chosen in Constantinople without them. It is the sort of conversation soldiers have when an emperor is dying and no heir has been named. Theodora treats it as treason against a living man. Both are recalled from the eastern command to the capital and put to answer for it, and the answering is done before Justinian is well enough to be told.
suggested_refs: The eastern field command in 542, held jointly by Belisarius and Bouzes
sources: Procopius, Secret History 4, as characterized in the DIR biography

stops.name: The Great Palace, the room under the floor
stops.date_confidence: single-source hostile allegation, and dated only by inference from the 542 episode. The Secret History is Procopius's private invective; no independent record of any such confinement survives, and there is nothing to check it against.
stops.campa: Bouzes is put, Procopius says, into an underground chamber of the palace where no light comes and nobody speaks, and kept there more than two years, fed by a mute, until he comes out half blind and unable to stand. Belisarius keeps his life and loses his household, his guards, and his money, and is restored a year later when Antonina asks for it. There is no prison register for any of this. There is one man's book, written in hatred, and no second witness.
stops.quote: guard the prisoner as securely as possible and forbidding him to speak of the matter to anyone until either the Empress should take pity on the poor wretch, or... he should at last end his days.
suggested_refs: The substructures of the Great Palace of Constantinople, partly excavated under Sultanahmet
sources: Procopius, Secret History 4 and 16, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: The Great Palace, the strap about the ears
stops.date_confidence: single-source hostile allegation from Secret History 16, undated in the text; the date orders the segment only. One correction to the research pool: within the Diogenes affair the strap is applied to Theodore, an associate of Diogenes, and not to Diogenes himself.
stops.campa: A young man named Diogenes, well liked in the city, is to be destroyed, and the case wants testimony. An associate of his called Theodore is taken up, and a leather strap is wound about his head at the level of the ears and twisted until it tightens. It is the plainest instrument in the world and it needs neither a room nor a machine. Procopius says the man believed his eyes had jumped out of his head, and still would not say what was wanted of him. The charge against Diogenes fails. No date attaches to any of it and no document of the proceeding survives, only the scene and the two names.
stops.quote: she caused the attendants to wind a leathern strap on the man's head, about his ears, and then ordered them to twist and so to tighten the strap.
stops.quote_source: Procopius, Secret History (Anecdota) 16, the Diogenes affair
suggested_refs: Secret History 16, the Diogenes affair and the interrogation of Theodore
sources: Procopius, Secret History 16, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: The Palace of Hormisdas, the bishop with no see
stops.date_confidence: the consecration is dated 543/544 and takes place at Constantinople, performed by Theodosius of Alexandria at the urging of Theodora and the Ghassanid king al-Harith ibn Jabalah; the research pool's 542/543 is a year early. The venue is not documented: Jacob was resident at the monastery of Sykai, and this pin marks the house where Theodosius was living under Theodora's protection, not an attested site for the rite.
stops.campa: Theodosius of Alexandria, a patriarch with no city, living in an empress's outbuilding, lays hands on two monks: Jacob, called Baradaeus for the horse-blanket rags he goes about in, and Theodore. They are made bishops of nowhere in particular, with the whole East for a diocese. Jacob will walk it for decades dressed as a beggar, ordaining priests ahead of the police, and the church that survives him still carries his nickname. Theodora and the Arab king al-Harith asked for the consecration.
suggested_refs: The Syriac Orthodox hierarchy descended from the ordinations of Jacob Baradaeus
sources: John of Ephesus, as summarized in the DIR biography
Wikipedia, 'Jacob Baradaeus' (for the 543/544 date and the role of al-Harith)

stops.name: The Great Palace, the race for Nobadia
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. John of Ephesus is the only source and is a partisan Miaphysite; the Julian mission is conventionally dated 543, and recent scholarship revisits his chronology. Theodora never travelled to Nubia; the stop is sited where the order was given.
stops.campa: Two missions set out for the Nubian kingdom above the first cataract, one from the emperor carrying the Chalcedonian creed and one from the empress carrying the other. John of Ephesus says she wrote ahead to the duke of the Thebaid, telling him plainly what would happen to him if the emperor's party crossed first, and that the duke discovered reasons for delay. Julian reaches the Nobadae first, and the king above the first cataract is baptised into the creed the emperor's own law condemns. The Chalcedonian party arrives to find the work done.
suggested_refs: The kingdom of Nobadia between the first and third cataracts, converted by the mission of Julian
sources: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History, as summarized in the DIR biography and the research dossier

stops.name: The Great Palace, the daughter nobody names
stops.date_confidence: the existence of the daughter and the grandsons is reported by John of Ephesus; no date attaches, and 0545 orders the segment. The daughter's name, and the identity of her father, are absent from every surviving source.
stops.campa: John of Ephesus mentions in passing, and only the once, that the empress has a daughter, born before the marriage, and neither her name nor her father is written down anywhere that survives. He mentions grandsons: an Anastasius who appears in the Miaphysite church quarrels, a John described as consul and ambassador. So the daughter of the theatre years is in the record only sideways, as the mother of men who are named. Who her father was, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The prosopography of Theodora's kin in John of Ephesus and the sixth-century Constantinopolitan record
sources: John of Ephesus, as summarized in the DIR biography and a University of Helsinki research summary

stops.name: The Great Palace, the niece and the heir
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Victor of Tunnuna attests the kinship between Sophia and Theodora, but does not specify which sister was Sophia's mother, and the date of her marriage to Justin is not fixed in the sources consulted; 0546 orders the segment.
stops.campa: Sophia, daughter of one of Theodora's sisters, is married to Justin, son of Justinian's sister, and the two houses are stitched together at the level of the next generation. Victor of Tunnuna records the kinship and does not say which sister was her mother, so the aunt is either the empress on the stage or the general's wife. When Justinian dies in 565 that couple takes the throne, and the bear-keeper's line sits in the purple a second time, in a woman who will govern in her husband's name through his madness. Theodora is seventeen years dead by then.
suggested_refs: The reign of Justin II and the empress Sophia, 565-578
sources: Victor of Tunnuna, as cited in the DIR entry on Sophia (roman-emperors.sites.luc.edu/sophia.htm)

stops.name: San Vitale, the panel in the apse
stops.date_confidence: the panel is dated to the completion of the church, consecrated in 547 by Bishop Maximian. Theodora never travelled to Ravenna and is not recorded anywhere west of the Adriatic at any point in her life: this pin marks the image, not a visit, and popular captions describing her as present at the dedication are wrong. A minority view, argued from the tesserae of the imperial panels, dates the work after her death in 548 and is not widely accepted. The Smarthistory essay and the UNESCO listing page both returned errors and could not be read directly.
stops.campa: In the apse of a church in Ravenna paid for by a banker called Julius Argentarius, in a city her husband's armies took seven years ago, the empress stands in porphyry purple, crowned and haloed, holding out a gold chalice. She has never been within a thousand miles of the place, and this is the only certain likeness of her face. On the hem of her mantle the three Magi carry their gifts up toward the chalice, so that she stands at the end of a procession of offering that began at Bethlehem. Her court women are ranged behind her. At her feet a fountain runs.
suggested_refs: The apse mosaic panels of Justinian and Theodora, Basilica of San Vitale, Ravenna, consecrated 547
sources: Wikipedia, 'Basilica of San Vitale'
Irina Andreescu-Treadgold and Warren Treadgold, 'Procopius and the Imperial Panels of S. Vitale', The Art Bulletin 79 (1997), cited from the dossier bibliography; the JSTOR record could not be opened

stops.name: The Great Palace, the plague of cancer
stops.date_confidence: 28 June 548 is the conventional scholarly date. The translation of Victor of Tunnuna consulted enters the notice under the chronicle year 549; that discrepancy between the fetched text and the widely cited modern date is left standing here rather than resolved. The retrospective diagnosis of breast cancer is a modern specification the Latin does not support.
stops.campa: She dies in the palace at about fifty, of something a Latin chronicler calls a plague of cancer spread through the whole body. The man who records it is a Chalcedonian who calls her the enemy of the synod and cannot keep the wonder out of the sentence. Later retellings name the breast; the word in the source names no organ at all, and the careful study of the phrasing cannot get past that. Justinian has seventeen years of reign in front of him and does not marry again.
stops.quote: Theodora Augusta, the enemy of the Chalcedonian synod, came to the end of her life in a wondrous way as the plague of cancer had spread throughout her whole body.
stops.quote_source: Victor of Tunnuna, Chronicon, s.a. 549, recording the death of 548, trans. Aymenn al-Tamimi
suggested_refs: Victor of Tunnuna's Chronicon, the hostile Chalcedonian notice of her death
sources: Victor of Tunnuna, Chronicon, English translation at aymennaltamimi.com
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Church of the Holy Apostles, the porphyry sarcophagus
stops.date_confidence: the burial follows the death; the day is not documented. The coordinate is corrected to 41.0197, 28.9497, the Fatih Mosque site: the research pool's afterlife lens carried 41.0298, about 1.1 km north, disagreeing with its own geography lens. One tension is left standing: the rebuilt church was consecrated on 28 June 550, two years after her death, so she was either interred before that consecration or translated into the mausoleum afterward.
stops.campa: They carry her to the Church of the Holy Apostles, Constantine's own foundation and the burial place of the emperors, and lay her in a sarcophagus of imperial porphyry in the mausoleum at the end of the northern arm. Justinian is brought into the same room seventeen years later. In 1204 the crusaders open the imperial tombs for the gold, and Niketas Choniates records that not even Justinian's was spared. The church itself comes down in the 1460s for the Fatih Mosque. Sixth-century porphyry sarcophagi stand in the open air beside a museum in Istanbul now, uninscribed, and none of them can be identified as hers.
suggested_refs: The porphyry imperial sarcophagi outside the Istanbul Archaeological Museums and in the atrium of Hagia Eirene, none inscribed
sources: Wikipedia, 'Church of the Holy Apostles', citing Niketas Choniates
Geoffrey Greatrex, De Imperatoribus Romanis, 'Theodora'

stops.name: The Church of the Holy Apostles, the candles
stops.date_confidence: attested for a procession of 559 by the tenth-century De Ceremoniis of Constantine VII; the day is not given and the tenth-century text was not independently fetched for this file.
stops.campa: Eleven years after her death a procession goes out to the Church of the Holy Apostles. Justinian is an old man by now and has six years of reign left, all of them alone. A book of ceremonial compiled four centuries afterward still sets down the order of that day, and the order includes the halt. The tomb is in the mausoleum at the end of the northern arm, where he will be laid himself. The emperor turns aside to it, and lights candles there, and then the procession goes on to the rest of the day.
suggested_refs: Constantine VII, De Ceremoniis, recording the imperial procession of 559 to the Holy Apostles
sources: Constantine VII, De Ceremoniis, as summarized in the research dossier
Wikipedia, 'Theodora (6th century)'
